chunks.text: 2 Methodology Fig. 1 provides an overview of the proposed framework. Given a rectified stereo microscopic video, the objective is to combine RGB appearance and depth-derived geometric information from individual surgical instruments and the surrounding anatomy for surgical skill assessment. To achieve this, the framework first reconstructs a dense metric representation of the surgical scene by combining stereo and monocular depth estimation. The reconstructed scene is then decomposed into semantically meaningful regions corresponding to the surgical instruments and surrounding anatomy. Finally, RGB appearance, geometric depth, and instrument motion are jointly encoded through a hierarchical attention architecture to predict surgical skill. Unlike conventional video-based methods that operate solely on monocular RGB images, the proposed approach incorporates depth-derived geometric information, enabling the model to explicitly capture discriminative instrument appearance, scene geometry, and instrument-tissue interactions. 2.1 Dense Metric Foreground Reconstruction Instrument Segmentation and Mask Propagation The first frame of each video is initialized using prompt-based segmentation. Sparse prompts are provided to the Segment Anything Model (SAM) [ 9 ] to segment the grasper, scissors, and visible foreground anatomy. These initial masks establish the semantic identities of the three scene components used by the downstream model. The first-frame masks are propagated through the complete sequence using CUTIE [ 2 ] , producing frame-wise semantic masks { M t , k } t = 1 T \{M_{t,k}\}_{t=1}^{T} for each stream k ∈ 𝒦 k\in\mathcal{K} . Here, M t , k ∈ { 0 , 1 } H × W M_{t,k}\in\{0,1\}^{H\times W} identifies the image region associated with the grasper, scissors, or anatomy at frame t t . The propagated masks are used to isolate the corresponding RGB and depth information for semantic feature extraction.

Figure 2: Overview of the proposed depth-guided semantic feature extraction pipeline. The first frame of each microscopic stereo video is annotated using prompt-based segmentation, and the resulting instrument and foreground masks are propagated throughout the sequence. Stereo depth provides sparse metric measurements, while monocular depth provides dense relative structure. The two estimates are aligned within the foreground region to recover dense metric depth. Semantic RGB and depth features are then extracted separately for the grasper, scissors, and anatomy streams and used for temporal skill assessment. Dense Metric Depth Estimation For each rectified stereo pair ( I t L , I t R ) (I_{t}^{L},I_{t}^{R}) , we estimate an initial metric stereo depth map Z t s , ℓ Z_{t}^{s,\ell} for view ℓ ∈ { L , R } \ell\in\{L,R\} using the OpenCV block-matching stereo implementation [ 15 ] . From the resulting disparity map, we construct a binary validity mask C t ℓ C_{t}^{\ell} by retaining pixels with positive disparity estimates and rejecting zero or invalid disparities. Valid stereo measurements are subsequently restricted to the segmented operative region during metric alignment, such that only correspondences within the region of interest are retained. Because stereo matching can be incomplete or noisy in microscopic surgical scenes, these measurements are treated as sparse metric depth references rather than a dense reconstruction. In parallel, a dense relative depth map Z t m , ℓ Z_{t}^{m,\ell} is estimated using Depth Anything V2 [ 21 ] . Reliable foreground pixels used for metric alignment are defined as Ω t ℓ = { 𝐩 | M t ℓ ( 𝐩 ) = 1 , C t ℓ ( 𝐩 ) = 1 } , \Omega_{t}^{\ell}=\left\{\mathbf{p}\;\middle|\;M_{t}^{\ell}(\mathbf{p})=1,\;C_{t}^{\ell}(\mathbf{p})=1\right\}, (1) where 𝐩 = ( u , v ) \mathbf{p}=(u,v) denotes an image pixel, M t ℓ M_{t}^{\ell} denotes the segmented operative-region mask, and C t ℓ C_{t}^{\ell} denotes the binary stereo validity mask.

The dense metric depth map is then obtained as Z ^ t ℓ ​ ( 𝐩 ) = α t ℓ ​ Z t m , ℓ ​ ( 𝐩 ) + β t ℓ . \hat{Z}_{t}^{\ell}(\mathbf{p})=\alpha_{t}^{\ell}Z_{t}^{m,\ell}(\mathbf{p})+\beta_{t}^{\ell}. (2) This preserves the metric scale provided by stereo while using monocular depth to fill regions where stereo matching is unreliable or unavailable. 2.2 Semantic-Stream Skill Representation Rather than organizing the representation only by feature modality, we decompose each frame into three semantically meaningful scene components: 𝒦 = { grasper , scissors , anatomy } . \mathcal{K}=\{\mathrm{grasper},\mathrm{scissors},\mathrm{anatomy}\}. (3) Each stream contains the visual appearance and geometric information associated with its corresponding operative element. This organization allows the learned attention and score patterns to be interpreted according to instrument role and anatomical context. Let 𝐱 t , k r \mathbf{x}^{r}_{t,k} and 𝐱 t , k d \mathbf{x}^{d}_{t,k} denote the RGB and depth features at frame t t for semantic stream k k . Because the two modalities have different dimensions and statistical properties, they are projected into compatible latent spaces: 𝐫 t , k = ϕ r , k ​ ( 𝐱 t , k r ) , 𝐝 t , k = ϕ d , k ​ ( 𝐱 t , k d ) , k ∈ 𝒦 . \mathbf{r}_{t,k}=\phi_{r,k}\left(\mathbf{x}^{r}_{t,k}\right),\qquad\mathbf{d}_{t,k}=\phi_{d,k}\left(\mathbf{x}^{d}_{t,k}\right),\qquad k\in\mathcal{K}. (4) Semantic-Stream Fusion The projected RGB and depth features are fused independently within each semantic stream: 𝐮 t , k = ϕ f , k ​ ( [ 𝐫 t , k ; 𝐝 t , k ] ) , k ∈ 𝒦 . \mathbf{u}_{t,k}=\phi_{f,k}\left(\left[\mathbf{r}_{t,k};\mathbf{d}_{t,k}\right]\right),\qquad k\in\mathcal{K}. (5) The frame-level representations of stream k k are collected into 𝐔 k = [ 𝐮 1 , k , … , 𝐮 T , k ] . \mathbf{U}_{k}=\left[\mathbf{u}_{1,k},\ldots,\mathbf{u}_{T,k}\right].

(6) Per-Stream Temporal Encoding Surgical skill is expressed through temporally evolving patterns of instrument control and tool–anatomy interaction. Each fused semantic stream is therefore processed by an independent dilated temporal convolutional network: 𝐡 t , k = f TCN , k ​ ( 𝐮 1 , k , … , 𝐮 T , k ) t , \mathbf{h}_{t,k}=f_{\mathrm{TCN},k}\left(\mathbf{u}_{1,k},\ldots,\mathbf{u}_{T,k}\right)_{t}, (7) where 𝐡 t , k ∈ ℝ d tcn \mathbf{h}_{t,k}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{tcn}}} is the temporally encoded representation of stream k k at frame t t . Using a dedicated temporal convolutional network (TCN) for each semantic stream allows the grasper, scissors, and anatomy branches to learn distinct temporal dynamics before global fusion. Local Skill Score A stream-specific multilayer perceptron (MLP) score head is applied to each temporally encoded feature: s t , k = MLP s , k ​ ( 𝐡 t , k ) , s_{t,k}=\mathrm{MLP}_{s,k}\left(\mathbf{h}_{t,k}\right), (8) where s t , k s_{t,k} denotes the local skill score produced by stream k k at frame t t . Each stream also learns an independent temporal-attention distribution: α t , k = exp ⁡ ( MLP α , k ​ ( 𝐡 t , k ) ) ∑ τ = 1 T exp ⁡ ( MLP α , k ​ ( 𝐡 τ , k ) ) . \alpha_{t,k}=\frac{\exp\left(\mathrm{MLP}_{\alpha,k}\left(\mathbf{h}_{t,k}\right)\right)}{\sum_{\tau=1}^{T}\exp\left(\mathrm{MLP}_{\alpha,k}\left(\mathbf{h}_{\tau,k}\right)\right)}. (9) The normalization is performed over time within each stream, such that ∑ t = 1 T α t , k = 1 , ∀ k ∈ 𝒦 . \sum_{t=1}^{T}\alpha_{t,k}=1,\qquad\forall k\in\mathcal{K}. (10) The local temporal attention α t , k \alpha_{t,k} identifies the frames that are most informative within stream k k and is used to form the auxiliary stream-level prediction: y ^ k = ∑ t = 1 T α t , k ​ s t , k . \hat{y}_{k}=\sum_{t=1}^{T}\alpha_{t,k}s_{t,k}. (11) Frame-Wise Semantic Stream Attention The relative importance of the grasper, scissors, and anatomy streams may vary throughout a trial.

Stream attention is therefore computed directly from the temporally encoded features: γ t , k = exp ⁡ ( MLP γ ​ ( 𝐡 t , k ) ) ∑ j ∈ 𝒦 exp ⁡ ( MLP γ ​ ( 𝐡 t , j ) ) . \gamma_{t,k}=\frac{\exp\left(\mathrm{MLP}_{\gamma}\left(\mathbf{h}_{t,k}\right)\right)}{\sum_{j\in\mathcal{K}}\exp\left(\mathrm{MLP}_{\gamma}\left(\mathbf{h}_{t,j}\right)\right)}. (12) The normalization is performed across semantic streams at each frame: ∑ k ∈ 𝒦 γ t , k = 1 , ∀ t . \sum_{k\in\mathcal{K}}\gamma_{t,k}=1,\qquad\forall t. (13) Thus, γ t , k \gamma_{t,k} represents the relative emphasis placed on stream k k at frame t t . In contrast, α t , k \alpha_{t,k} is normalized over time and represents the temporal importance of frame t t within stream k k . Global Stream Fusion and Temporal Attention The semantic representations are fused at each frame using the learned stream-attention weights: 𝐡 ¯ t = ∑ k ∈ 𝒦 γ t , k ​ 𝐡 t , k . \bar{\mathbf{h}}_{t}=\sum_{k\in\mathcal{K}}\gamma_{t,k}\mathbf{h}_{t,k}. (14) This produces the globally fused temporal sequence 𝐇 ¯ = [ 𝐡 ¯ 1 , … , 𝐡 ¯ T ] . \bar{\mathbf{H}}=\left[\bar{\mathbf{h}}_{1},\ldots,\bar{\mathbf{h}}_{T}\right]. (15) A separate global temporal-attention network is then applied to the fused sequence: e t global = h α ​ ( 𝐡 ¯ t ) . e_{t}^{\mathrm{global}}=h_{\alpha}\left(\bar{\mathbf{h}}_{t}\right). (16) The global temporal logits are normalized across the complete trial: α t = exp ⁡ ( e t global ) ∑ τ = 1 T exp ⁡ ( e τ global ) . \alpha_{t}=\frac{\exp\left(e_{t}^{\mathrm{global}}\right)}{\sum_{\tau=1}^{T}\exp\left(e_{\tau}^{\mathrm{global}}\right)}. (17) Therefore, ∑ t = 1 T α t = 1 . \sum_{t=1}^{T}\alpha_{t}=1. (18) The global temporal attention α t \alpha_{t} measures the importance of frame t t after information from the grasper, scissors, and anatomy streams has already been combined. It is learned independently from the local stream-specific attention α t , k \alpha_{t,k} .

Trial-Level Skill Prediction The final trial-level prediction combines the local skill score with the global temporal and frame-wise stream-attention weights: y ^ = ∑ t = 1 T ∑ k ∈ 𝒦 α t ​ γ t , k ​ s t , k . \hat{y}=\sum_{t=1}^{T}\sum_{k\in\mathcal{K}}\alpha_{t}\gamma_{t,k}s_{t,k}. (19) Here, s t , k s_{t,k} denotes the skill score produced by stream k k at frame t t , γ t , k \gamma_{t,k} determines the relative importance of that stream within the frame, and α t \alpha_{t} determines the importance of the fused frame within the complete trial. The effective contribution of stream k k at frame t t is therefore c t , k = α t ​ γ t , k ​ s t , k . c_{t,k}=\alpha_{t}\gamma_{t,k}s_{t,k}. (20) Importantly, the local temporal attention α t , k \alpha_{t,k} is not multiplied into the final global prediction. Instead, it is used to construct the auxiliary prediction y ^ k \hat{y}_{k} for each individual stream, whereas the final prediction uses the global temporal attention α t \alpha_{t} learned from the stream-fused representation. Training Objective The global prediction is supervised using the mean-squared error (MSE): ℒ fusion = MSE ⁡ ( y ^ , y ) . \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{fusion}}=\mathrm{MSE}\left(\hat{y},y\right). (21) To encourage every semantic branch to preserve independently discriminative skill information, the auxiliary stream predictions are also supervised: ℒ stream = 1 | 𝒦 | ​ ∑ k ∈ 𝒦 MSE ⁡ ( y ^ k , y ) . \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{stream}}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{K}|}\sum_{k\in\mathcal{K}}\mathrm{MSE}\left(\hat{y}_{k},y\right). (22) The complete training objective is ℒ = ℒ fusion + ℒ stream , \mathcal{L}=\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{fusion}}+\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{stream}}, (23) The fused loss optimizes the final video-level prediction, while the per-stream auxiliary loss encourages each semantic stream to retain independently discriminative skill information rather than relying entirely on the global fusion pathway.

Warmer colors indicate greater spatial attention. 3 Experiments and Results Dataset The dataset contains 33 videos of laryngeal microsurgery recorded using a stereo surgical microscope. Each video consists of synchronized left- and right-view microscopic video sequences of the same procedure. The videos had a mean duration of 47.6 ± 16.5 47.6\pm 16.5 s, with a range of 22.8–79.0 s and a total recording duration of 26.16 min. The surgical procedures were performed by six surgeons representing two professional training levels: three attending (expert) surgeons and three surgical residents. The dataset contains 15 procedures performed by the attending surgeons and 18 procedures performed by the residents, as summarized in Table 1 . Two surgical instruments are present in the operative scene: a grasper and a pair of scissors. Because either instrument may appear on the left or right side of the image, each video includes tool-identity annotations that map the left- and right-side instrument regions to the grasper and scissors. These annotations allow instrument-specific representations to be organized consistently across videos. Table 1: Participant composition of the laryngeal microsurgery dataset.

Task definition, training, and evaluation. Using the participant-level training designations, we formulate surgical skill assessment as a binary classification task between attending surgeons and surgical residents. Each video is labeled according to the training level of the participant, with resident videos assigned y = 0 y=0 and expert videos assigned y = 1 y=1 . The ground-truth label therefore reflects the participant’s training status rather than a video-specific performance score.

During training, the model learns a scalar video-level output y ^ \hat{y} using the objective in Eq. 23 . MSE is used as a regression surrogate for the binary expertise label rather than to estimate a continuous surgical-skill score. For evaluation, we performed leave-one-surgeon-out cross validation. All six participant-disjoint folds used the same fixed training settings: AdamW for 20 epochs with learning rate 2 × 10 − 4 2\times 10^{-4} , batch size 1, weight decay 1 × 10 − 4 1\times 10^{-4} , and cosine annealing to 1 × 10 − 5 1\times 10^{-5} . Model selection and training settings were kept fixed across all folds, with no inner validation split or fold-specific hyperparameter tuning. At inference, the scalar output is converted to a binary prediction using a fixed midpoint threshold. A video score is classified as expert if y ^ ≥ 0.5 \hat{y}\geq 0.5 and as resident otherwise. This threshold was specified a priori and was not tuned on the evaluation data. We report expert-class precision, recall, and F1-score, together with overall classification accuracy, under this decision rule. Table 3: Evaluation results of leave-one-surgeon-out cross-validation. Best values are shown in bold. NB: ∗ USSA (RGB) [ 12 ] predicted all trials as resident, resulting in zero precision, recall, and F1 for the expert class. The RGB model uses features extracted independently from the grasper, scissors, and anatomy regions. Depth features were encoded using either spatial pyramid pooling (SPP) or atrous spatial pyramid pooling (ASPP), and the proposed multimodal model combines semantic RGB with SPP-based depth features.

We additionally ablated semantic decomposition, temporal attention, and auxiliary supervision. All proposed-model variants and ablations were evaluated using the same participant-disjoint leave-one-participant-out protocol. For comparison with prior work, we adapted the publicly available Unified Surgical Skill Assessment (USSA) framework [ 12 ] as a full-frame RGB baseline and evaluated it using the same six participant-disjoint folds, trial labels, and pooled out-of-fold metrics, with predictions thresholded at 0.5. Role of dense 3D scene information The primary objective of this work is to investigate whether incorporating dense metric three-dimensional scene information improves video-based surgical skill assessment. Table 3 compares the performance of the different semantic-stream representations under the participant-disjoint evaluation protocol. The results show that the proposed combination of semantic RGB with SPP-based depth achieves the strongest overall performance, with the lowest MAE and highest F1 score. SPP-based depth alone also performs strongly, whereas the ASPP depth representation is less effective, indicating that the benefit of geometric information depends on how it is encoded. These results suggest that reconstructed depth provides complementary geometric information rather than replacing visual appearance. While RGB features encode instrument and tissue appearance, dense metric depth provides information about instrument positioning and spatial relationships within the surgical field. Their combination therefore provides a richer representation of microsurgical performance than either modality alone. The architectural ablations in Table 3 further indicate that the complete model benefits from semantic decomposition, temporal attention, and auxiliary supervision. Removing semantic decomposition resulted in the largest performance decrease, with the F1 score dropping from 0.938 to 0.343.

Removing temporal attention and auxiliary supervision reduced the F1 score to 0.652 and 0.533, respectively. These results suggest that each component contributes to the overall performance of the framework under the participant-disjoint evaluation setting. The participant-wise results in Table 4 provide additional detail on performance across the held-out surgeons. In comparison, the adapted USSA baseline performs poorly on the held-out expert trials and predicts them predominantly as resident cases under this evaluation setting. This suggests that full-frame RGB features alone may be less robust to participant-level variation in this dataset. Table 5: Average per-frame semantic-component attention. Semantic RGB places the greatest attention on the grasper stream, whereas the depth-based representations distribute attention more broadly across instruments and anatomy; in particular, ASPP produces a relatively balanced distribution across the three streams. The proposed SPP + RGB model, which achieves the strongest overall performance in Table 3 , shifts attention toward anatomy ( 0.47 ± 0.38 0.47\pm 0.38 ) and scissors ( 0.28 ± 0.36 0.28\pm 0.36 ), while reducing the grasper contribution ( 0.24 ± 0.37 0.24\pm 0.37 ).

This redistribution is consistent with the nature of laryngeal microsurgery, where skill depends strongly on fine-grained scissors–tissue interactions during precise tissue cutting. Table 6 shows that the location of the global temporal-attention peak varies substantially across representations. Semantic RGB and ASPP depth produce broadly distributed peak locations for both experts and residents. In contrast, SPP depth exhibits a strong end-of-sequence preference for resident trials ( 0.99 ± 0.01 0.99\pm 0.01 ), while expert peaks remain substantially earlier ( 0.49 ± 0.26 0.49\pm 0.26 ). When SPP depth is combined with Semantic RGB, the resident peak shifts away from the sequence boundary to 0.59 ± 0.36 0.59\pm 0.36 , with a comparable distribution for experts ( 0.57 ± 0.44 0.57\pm 0.44 ). This suggests that multimodal fusion mitigates the pronounced terminal attention bias observed with SPP depth alone and yields a more balanced temporal representation across expertise groups. Semantic and spatial attention To further examine how semantic information contributes around highly attended temporal regions, Fig. 5 shows the stream-weighted local scores aligned to the peak temporal-attention frame. Expert trials exhibit a pronounced anatomy contribution around the attention peak, while the grasper and scissors contributions remain comparatively small. In contrast, resident trials show lower-magnitude and more evenly distributed contributions across the three semantic streams, with the scissors stream contributing modestly more than the grasper and anatomy streams. These patterns suggest that highly attended regions in expert trials are more strongly associated with anatomical context, whereas resident predictions rely on a more distributed combination of semantic features. We further examine the spatial distribution of attention in Fig. 3 , which presents four representative trials, including two expert and two resident examples. An attending otolaryngologist who did not participate in the recorded trials independently reviewed these representative attention maps and identified the instrument tip and instrument pivoting region as prominent areas of model attention. The attending surgeon considered these spatial regions clinically plausible in the context of instrument–tissue interaction and instrument stabilization by pivoting it on the laryngoscope, which are both relevant for surgical task execution. The RGB model uses features extracted independently from the grasper, scissors, and anatomy regions.

Depth features were encoded using either spatial pyramid pooling (SPP) or atrous spatial pyramid pooling (ASPP), and the proposed multimodal model combines semantic RGB with SPP-based depth features. We additionally ablated semantic decomposition, temporal attention, and auxiliary supervision. All proposed-model variants and ablations were evaluated using the same participant-disjoint leave-one-participant-out protocol. For comparison with prior work, we adapted the publicly available Unified Surgical Skill Assessment (USSA) framework [ 12 ] as a full-frame RGB baseline and evaluated it using the same six participant-disjoint folds, trial labels, and pooled out-of-fold metrics, with predictions thresholded at 0.5. 4 Conclusions This work presented a semantic RGB–depth approach for automated surgical skill assessment from microscopic stereo videos. The proposed approach incorporates dense depth representation of the surgical scene by combining sparse stereo depth with dense monocular depth estimates through a regression-based depth-fusion strategy. The reconstructed geometric representation is integrated with semantically decomposed RGB streams using a hierarchical attention architecture that jointly models instrument appearance, scene geometry, instrument motion, and instrument–tissue interactions. Evaluation on a dataset comprising of exvivo transoral microlaryngeal procedures using leave-one-surgeon-out validation showed that depth-derived geometric information provides complementary information for skill assessment beyond RGB appearance alone. The semantic representation further enables qualitative examination of spatial, temporal, and semantic attention patterns. An expert surgeon considered the observed spatial attention patterns clinically plausible, noting greater scissors attention near tool–tissue interaction regions and greater grasper attention near pivoting regions.

These attention patterns are interpreted as qualitative visualizations of learned model weighting; we acknowledge that causality between the highlighted regions and the predicted skill level cannot be directly established from attention weights alone. Although this study focused on exvivo transoral microlaryngeal surgery from a single dataset, the proposed framework may provide a basis for extending RGB–depth skill assessment to other microscope-guided procedures in which stereo video is available. A limitation of the present study is that the reconstructed depth was not evaluated against dense per-pixel metric ground truth. Future work will investigate validation using more comprehensive geometric ground truth, as well as larger, multi-institutional and invivo datasets. We will also examine whether highly attended regions exert greater influence on model predictions under controlled perturbations. Additional directions include self-supervised learning from unlabeled surgical videos, continuous skill scoring, and real-time intraoperative feedback.
